# Filtering searches by file type

When you search a big project, most of the noise comes from files you never
meant to search: lockfiles, minified JavaScript, vendored dependencies,
generated docs. ripgrep already skips a lot of that automatically by reading
your `.gitignore` files. The `--type` family of flags gives you a second,
manual layer of control: search only the kinds of files you actually care
about, by name, instead of typing out glob patterns every time.

There are four flags in this family: `--type` to include a file type,
`--type-not` to exclude one, `--type-add` to define your own, and
`--type-list` to see what's available.

## `--type`: search only this kind of file

Say you're in ripgrep's own source tree and you want to find `fn run`, but
only in Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

`--type` has the short form `-t`, and the type name can be glued right onto
it: `rg 'fn run' -trust`.

A "type" is just a name attached to one or more glob patterns. `rust` means
"files matching `*.rs`". Some types cover more ground than a single
extension — `c`, for example, matches both `*.c` and `*.h`, so `rg 'int
main' -tc` covers headers and source files at once. You can pass `--type`
more than once; each one adds to the set of types searched, so `-trust
-tpython` searches Rust files and Python files together.

## `--type-not`: search everything except this kind of file

`--type-not` (short form `-T`) does the opposite: it excludes a file type
instead of including it. `rg clap --type-not rust`, or more succinctly `rg
clap -Trust`, searches everywhere except Rust files. The pattern is the
same for both flags: `-t` means "include files of this type", `-T` means
"exclude files of this type." You can mix them in one command and repeat
either as many times as you need — `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` excludes Rust and
JSON files while including TOML files.

### The special `all` type

Both flags accept the special name `all`, standing in for every type
ripgrep knows about, including any you've defined for that command.
`--type all` puts ripgrep into a whitelist mode, searching only files it
recognizes as belonging to some type. `--type-not all` is the reverse: it
searches only files that don't match any known type.

The difference shows up on files with no telling extension. Say your
directory has a shell script named `my-shell-script` that sources a library
named `my-shell-library.bash`. The `sh` type's globs don't match
extension-less files, so both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` match only
`my-shell-library.bash` — `my-shell-script` isn't recognized as any type,
so whitelist mode skips it. `rg --type-not all` does the opposite: it
searches `my-shell-script`, precisely because that file is unrecognized,
and skips `my-shell-library.bash`.

`--type` and `--type-not` are also checked after `--glob` and after your
ignore files, so a glob or `.gitignore` rule that already ruled a file out
won't be overridden by a type flag.

## `--type-list`: see what types are defined, and what they match

`--type` and `--type-not` are only useful if you know what names are
available and what each one actually matches. `--type-list` prints them
all, one type per line, as a name followed by a comma-separated list of its
globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types, generally corresponding
to well-known file formats — `rust`, `c`, `cpp`, `python`, `make`, `json`,
and many more. Piping `--type-list` through `rg` yourself, as above, is a
quick way to check whether a type you're about to use covers the files you
expect.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

If you find yourself writing the same glob over and over, turn it into a
type. Say you often search "web" files — JavaScript, HTML, and CSS
together:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Each `--type-add` adds one glob to a type (give the same name more than
once and the globs accumulate); a glob can itself be a brace-expanded list,
as above. This defines a new type called `web` matching `*.{html,css,js}`,
then searches it with `-tweb` for the pattern `title`. Add `--type-list` to
the same command and `web` shows up alongside the built-in types, for that
command only. Type names may only contain Unicode letters and numbers — no
punctuation.

### Types you add don't stick around

`--type-add` (and its counterpart `--type-clear`, which removes the globs
already defined for a type so you can redefine it from scratch) applies
only to the command you ran. ripgrep doesn't save `web` anywhere, so it's
gone on your next invocation. To get it every time, either alias your
shell:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add it to a ripgrep configuration file (point the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`
environment variable at a file, then list flags in it, one per line):

```
# Add my 'web' type.
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}*
```

Either way, `--type-add` gets re-applied automatically on every run.

### Building a type out of other types

`--type-add` also understands an `include` directive, pulling in the globs
from other already-defined types instead of listing extensions by hand. To
define a `src` type covering C++, Python, and Markdown, then add one more
glob to it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

That's the toolkit: `--type` and `--type-not` to search in or around a set
of file types, `--type-list` to check what's defined, and `--type-add` to
teach ripgrep about a kind of file it doesn't already know.
